AI-assisted loan file preparation

SBA 7(a) first. A working application, shown on synthetic data.

The tool prepares the file. The underwriter decides.

Status: runs locally. No real borrower data, no real lender system, nothing deployed.

The problem

  • Commercial loan files are document-heavy: read statements, key figures, cross-check them, apply program rules, write the memo.
  • That work sits before the judgment call, and the judgment call is what experienced underwriters are for.
  • Hypothesis: prepare the file with sources attached, so underwriters spend their time deciding. Unproven until measured on real files.

Rules are tested code, not model output. Anything unknown or failing goes to a person. Approved files hand off to a mock lender servicing adapter.

Controls built in

  • Human decides: enforced in the database; only an underwriter acting as themselves can record a decision.
  • Evidence: no fact without a page and quote; accepted means faithfully extracted, not verified true.
  • Isolation: per-lender data separation enforced by the database; append-only, hash-chained audit log.
  • Safety: identifiers encrypted and redacted before any model call; document text is never treated as instructions.
  • Access: OpenID Connect sign-in, four roles, revocable sessions, every sign-in and admin change audited.
  • Hardening: upload checks with fail-closed malware scan, rate limits, scrubbed logs, security headers, threat model mapped to tests.

What it might be worth

ESTIMATE ONLY. Durations are our guesses, not measurements.

  • Modeled assisted-to-manual time ratio: 0.19 to 0.50 at middle assumptions.
  • At pessimistic assumptions the ratio exceeds 1.0 (no saving).
  • We make no savings claim. The first 30 days measure the real manual baseline with two of your underwriters.

Where it would run

  • Testing now: a hosted test deployment is prepared (Vercel with a hosted database) for non-sensitive synthetic testing only.
  • Pilot with real lender data: we recommend AWS containers, because the database must enforce lender separation, the malware scanner must run as a service, and the lender will ask where data lives. This is a recommendation; the decision is yours and your lender's.
  • Finding that shaped this: some hosted databases give default roles the ability to bypass row-level separation, and some connection poolers may break per-request lender settings. We test for both before any use.

What it is not yet

  • No real model, OCR, identity provider or hosting; no real documents tested. Sign-in is built to the OpenID Connect standard and tested with a stand-in provider.
  • Debt service covers the new loan only, with a placeholder rate; eligibility, collateral and credit reports are not evaluated.
  • No third-party security test, no lender vendor-risk review, and items awaiting counsel and compliance review. This is not legal advice.

Your requirements: what would make this a yes?

  1. Which lending lines and volumes first? What outcome defines success, and by when?
  2. Where do files and decisions live today; what integration is mandatory?
  3. Your credit policy overlays and pricing inputs.
  4. Vendor, cloud, data-residency and model-provider requirements; who approves vendor risk?
  5. Governance and examiner expectations; budget range; pilot sponsor and underwriters.
